title: Look at your own serve
body: Your team won 4 of the 10 rallies you served, against 9 of the 13 your partner served. Overall your team won 17 of 28 rallies on serve (61%), so the team's serving record is not weak overall.
try: Watch your six lost serves and ask: is it too high, too predictable, or is the third shot the problem? Change one thing next game (height, placement or the plan for the third shot) and count again. General advice, not tested by this video: mixing a short serve with a flick serve makes the receiver's first move harder to guess.
sure: How sure: low. Ten serves is a hint, not proof (p about 0.22), and who served is inferred from where the players stand.

title: Have a plan for the long rallies
body: Your team won 10 of 13 rallies under 6 s (77%) but only 19 of 39 longer ones (49%), and 8 of 17 over 10 s (47%). The video cannot show which shots were played.
try: Agree what you do when the first attack does not end the point: where you reset the rally (a clear to the back, a lift to the middle), and who covers the net. General advice; then check whether the long-rally record moves in your next game.
watch: Watch the long rallies you lost: 0:51 (R1, 18 s), 3:38 (R15, 14 s), 7:03 (R33, 19 s), 9:20 (R45, 12 s).
sure: How sure: low to medium. 13 short rallies against 39 longer ones, p about 0.11.

title: Ready stance: get lower
body: Your legs were nearly straight (knees not bent below 150 degrees) in 82% of the frames where you were near the camera; your typical knee angle was 166 degrees against 168 for your partner. Posture was the same in won and lost rallies (bent in 17% and 18% of frames).
try: General advice, not tested by this video: a bent-knee ready position usually gives a quicker first step. Next game, the share of bent-knee frames is the number to move.
watch: Watch your stance in any rally after 6:19, when you are on the near side of the court.
sure: How sure: medium for the measurement (1,926 frames of you in 25 rallies, near half only). Whether a lower stance wins you more points is not tested here.

title: A question for the video: stay compact?
body: You and your partner were within 1.5 m of each other 26% of the time in rallies you won and 16% in rallies you lost (p = 0.03). It is one of nine comparisons, so about one result like this is expected by chance, and on each half of the court alone it is not significant (p = 0.12 and 0.17).
try: Watch the clips and see whether being far apart left a gap the opponents used. If it did, agree who takes the middle.
watch: Watch the lost rallies where you two were furthest apart: 4:23 (R19), 1:12 (R2), 9:00 (R43), 9:20 (R45).
sure: How sure: lowest. One small p among nine; tracking is weakest when players overlap.

title: Your team wins the quick points
body: Your team won 10 of 13 rallies that ended within 6 seconds (77%).
try: Keep attacking the first loose ball. General advice: when a point is going your way early, do not slow it down.
sure: How sure: low to medium. 13 short rallies; p about 0.11.

title: Running is not what separates won from lost rallies
body: You covered 400 m, the most of the four players (your partner 392 m, the opponents 325 m and 377 m). Per rally you ran 8.0 m in won and 7.7 m in lost rallies, at 0.91 and 0.83 m/s, and spent 12% and 16% of the time at the back (all p above 0.2).
watch: Nothing to fix here: this is not a fitness problem.
sure: How sure: medium. Small effects could hide in 28 won and 23 lost rallies; far-court distances are rougher.

title: A steady game from start to finish
body: Your team won 7, 6, 8 and 8 of 13 rallies in the four quarters of the game. The score was tied 8 times with 7 lead changes, and your team led 29-23 before the last rally. Your best run was 6 points from 2:01.
watch: Watch your run from 2:01 (R6) to see what worked.
sure: How sure: high. This is read straight from the scoreboard.
